summary: Specifies the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO), which replaces the TCP MD5 Signature option of RFC 2385. It supports stronger message authentication codes, protects against replay on long-lived connections, and works with static or externally managed keys. It suits uses like BGP and LDP. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: A secret handshake stamped on every TCP message so no one can fake them. It is a newer and stronger stamp than the old one.

questions: how does tcp-ao prevent replay attacks
subtitle: A TCP option that stamps every segment with a keyed authentication code, replacing the old TCP MD5 signature.

tldr.problem: The TCP MD5 Signature option relies on a simple keyed hash that faces escalating attacks, and it has no key-change coordination or algorithm agility.
tldr.mechanism: TCP-AO adds a TCP option (Kind 29) with a KeyID, a RNextKeyID and a MAC. Per-connection traffic keys are derived from a Master Key Tuple, and a Sequence Number Extension guards against replay in long-lived connections.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5925 obsoletes RFC 2385 (TCP MD5). It does not negotiate keys or encrypt, so keys come from manual setup or an external protocol, and it is not meant to replace IPsec.

today: RFC 5925 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2385 (TCP MD5), and the unit metadata lists no later RFC obsoleting or updating it. Its algorithms are specified in RFC 5926.

sections.title: Why TCP MD5 Needed Replacing
sections.content:
The TCP MD5 Signature option authenticates TCP segments (the pseudoheader, TCP header and data). It was developed to protect BGP sessions from spoofed TCP segments that could affect BGP data or the connection itself.

The RFC lists the problems: MD5 is a simple keyed hash under escalating attack, and the option lacks both key management and algorithm agility. TCP-AO keeps the same goal but adds support for stronger hash functions, replay protection for long-lived connections, coordinated key changes and a clearer recommendation for external key management.

It is meant for current TCP MD5 uses such as BGP and LDP, and for any long-lived TCP connection, such as one between proxy caches. A given connection uses only one of the two mechanisms, and TCP MD5 connections cannot be migrated to TCP-AO.
sections.eli5: The old secret stamp could be copied by clever cheaters and could not be swapped for a new one easily. TCP-AO is a better stamp that can also be changed safely.

sections.title: The TCP-AO Option Format
sections.content:
TCP-AO uses TCP option Kind 29. After Kind and Length come two one-byte ID fields and then the MAC.

  • Length covers the whole option and must be at least 4; a shorter or inconsistent value means the segment is discarded.
  • KeyID names the Master Key Tuple used to make this segment's MAC. It has no cryptographic meaning and no value is reserved.
  • RNextKeyID tells the peer which key the sender is ready to use for segments it receives.
  • MAC is the authentication code. Typical MACs are 96 to 128 bits (12 to 16 bytes), but any length that fits is allowed.

The option does not say which MAC algorithm is used. That is part of the connection's configured security state. A segment must not carry more than one TCP-AO option, and a connection must not use both TCP-AO and TCP MD5; if both appear, TCP silently discards the segment.
sections.eli5: The stamp has a label for which secret was used, a hint about which secret to use next, and the stamp itself.

sections.title: Master Key Tuples and Traffic Keys
sections.content:
TCP-AO uses two kinds of keys. A Master Key Tuple (MKT) describes the settings for one or more connections: the TCP socket pair (which may use ranges, masks or wildcards), a flag for whether other TCP options are covered by the MAC, a SendID and a RecvID, the master key, the key derivation function (KDF) and the MAC algorithm. IDs may be any value from 0 to 255. The components of an MKT must not change during a connection, though the set of MKTs may.

From the MKT, each connection derives traffic keys, which are unidirectional. The KDF context combines the socket pair with the two endpoints' Initial Sequence Numbers (ISNs), so each connection instance gets unique keys even when a static MKT is reused. For a SYN segment the destination ISN is not yet known and zero is used. Up to four traffic keys exist per MKT (send and receive, for SYN and for other segments), but a typical connection uses three.

TCP-AO does not negotiate keys or parameters. It assumes manual setup or an out-of-band mechanism, and advises key lengths of 12 to 24 bytes and not sharing MKTs among multiple BGP peerings.
sections.eli5: There is one big secret kept in a safe, and from it each conversation makes its own small secret, so a stamp from one chat cannot be reused in another.

sections.title: Computing and Checking the MAC
sections.content:
The MAC is computed over, in order: the Sequence Number Extension, the IP pseudoheader, the TCP header (with the checksum and the TCP-AO MAC field set to zero) and the TCP data. Whether other TCP options are included depends on the MKT's option flag. The specific MAC and KDF algorithms are defined in RFC 5926, whose default MACs are truncated to 96 bits, which makes the whole option 16 bytes (two fewer than TCP MD5's 18).

On sending, TCP-AO is the last option processed. It finds the MKT for the connection, writes the KeyID from the current key's SendID and the RNextKeyID from the receive-next key's RecvID, computes the MAC and inserts it.

On receiving, it is the first option processed. TCP-AO finds the MKT from the socket pair and KeyID, checks the length, recomputes the MAC and silently discards the segment if it differs. If the received RNextKeyID differs from the current send key and that MKT is available, the receiver switches to it. Silent discards should be signaled to the user as a warning and be accessible through STATUS.
sections.eli5: The sender stamps each message using the secret and the message itself. The receiver makes the same stamp and, if it does not match, quietly throws the message away.

sections.title: Key Changes and Replay Protection
sections.content:
A connection can hold several MKTs at once, and the KeyID lets the receiver pick the right one without trying each key. The RNextKeyID field signals when a new key is ready, so a sender switches only when the peer can accept it and segments are not lost. Removing old keys is left to key management; TCP-AO provides no mechanism for it.

TCP sequence numbers are 32 bits and can roll over in a long-lived connection, which would let old segments repeat. TCP-AO therefore keeps a 32-bit Sequence Number Extension (SNE) for sent and received segments, both starting at zero, to emulate a 64-bit sequence space. The RFC gives an example algorithm that increments the SNE when the sequence number rolls over and copes with reordered segments, but the implementation is not mandated.
sections.eli5: Sequence numbers are like page numbers that start over after a very long book. The extension counts how many times the book restarted, so an old page cannot sneak back in.

sections.title: Resets, ICMP, Middleboxes and Legacy
sections.content:
Because a rebooted host has lost its traffic keys, TCP-AO can stop TCP resets from clearing old state on the peer. The RFC says connections using TCP-AO SHOULD also use TCP keepalives, and BGP connections SHOULD require graceful restart.

TCP-AO cannot authenticate ICMP. Implementations MUST by default ignore certain hard-error ICMP messages (ICMPv4 Type 3, Codes 2 to 4, and ICMPv6 Type 1, Codes 1 and 4) for synchronized connections that match an MKT.

TCP-AO cannot work natively across NAT/NAPT devices, which change addresses or ports. Middleboxes that modify TCP options may require the MKT to exclude options from the MAC, at some cost in protection. Systems supporting TCP MD5 MUST support TCP-AO, and SHOULD keep TCP MD5 only where legacy peers need it.
sections.eli5: Some helpers along the way change the envelope, which breaks the stamp. Careful settings let the stamp survive some helpers, but not ones that rewrite the address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Attackers who know the connection identifiers and the TCP-AO Length can send segments with invalid MACs to burn the receiver's processing effort. Off-path spoofing is easier than against IPsec, because typically only the source port is arbitrary.

TCP-AO includes the socket pair in the MAC, which prevents traffic-crossing attacks between connections sharing an MKT. It does not protect TCP congestion control from replays of authentic segments, and it does not encrypt. The RFC recommends IPsec and IKE where their richer protection or key management is wanted, and says TCP-AO may be used with TLS to complement it. IANA assigned TCP option 29 to TCP-AO.
sections.eli5: Cheaters can still make the receiver waste time checking fake stamps, and the stamp does not hide what is inside the message. For stronger protection, use the sturdier lock called IPsec.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Option length in bytes, at least 4.

fields.name: KeyID
fields.desc: Identifies the MKT used for this segment's MAC.

fields.name: RNextKeyID
fields.desc: The receive-next key the sender is ready to use.

fields.name: MAC
fields.desc: Authentication code; typical lengths are 96 to 128 bits.
